page.title: Day 10 against Neave's manual
page.standfirst_html: Every flag the comparator raised for Day 10, adjudicated against M.Day.10.16Feb22.pdf — the extracted text for wording, and twenty-two page images for numbers, colour-coded quote structure, and the decorative title-page banner pdftotext scrambles into “SECOND FIRST PROJECT”. The headline is a cluster of wrong cross-references around the same Scherkenbach “boxes and lines” diagram: one paragraph says “Day 9 page 9” in the source (confirmed against Day 9's own text, which independently corroborates “this is what any organisation is”) but reads “Day 9 page 2” on the site, while a second, later paragraph's bare self-reference to this same day's own page 3 was linked to Day 9 instead — wrong day, wrong anchor, in opposite directions. Elsewhere: a dropped Deming quote and its attribution clause (“the aim or purpose of the system is subjective“), a “1990”/“1992” version-year swap, a meaning-reversing “when do”/“when no” typo, a spurious “Chapter 18” inserted where the source has none, and Neave's own “wibble-wobble” callback broken by a substituted phrase. Decide each one; export the file; I make the edits and open the PR.

sections.title: Fix proposed
sections.note_html: Word-level defects, one dropped clause, one broken quote structure, a version-year swap, a meaning-reversing typo, and a pair of wrong-day cross-references that point in opposite directions around the same Scherkenbach diagram.

In order to give you plenty of ideas, I have sometimes written rather more than you could be expected to do in the limited amount of time available---so don't take my efforts as models!
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p1. Two changes in one sentence run: “have then included” loses “then”, and Neave's actual stated reason for over-writing — “In order to give you plenty of ideas” — is replaced with an invented “In each case”, which reads plausibly but is not what the source says.

items.proposal: So this is about what Dr Deming (amongst others) refers to as a "system" and describes as a "network". To illustrate this, William W Scherkenbach (a Director in Ford of America) drew the picture on [Day 9 page 9](../day-09/03-activity-9c-and-organisation-charts.qmd#sec-page9) and simply said: "This is what any organisation is!".

Day 9 page 2 (02-a-system.qmd#sec-page2) is a different section entirely and does not contain this diagram or quote. Four things changed in one sentence: the page number (2→9, wrong file and anchor), “in”→“of”, “picture”→“diagram”, and “any”→“my” — the last of which inverts the point (Scherkenbach's diagram is presented as a picture of organisations in general, not “my organisation” specifically).

items.chip: Dropped clause and attribution; Deming quote unmarked and misquoted
items.source_html: [There couldn't be a system if neither management nor their staff really understand what they are supposed to be trying to do, nor why! On what could they “work together”?] The aim is a value-judgment. [I.e. the aim or purpose of the system is subjective. As Deming said at the 1990 presentation to senior executives: “The aim of a system is not a theorem: you don't derive it from axioms and corollaries.” See Deming Speaks to European Executives, BDA Booklet A10 page 8 and DemDim page 265.]
items.site_html: [There couldn't be a system if neither management nor their staff really understand what they are supposed to be trying to do. On what could they “work together”?] The aim is a value-judgment. [i.e. the aim of the system is not a theorem: you don't derive it from axioms and corollaries.] See Deming Speaks to European Executives, BDA Booklet A10 page 8 and DemDim page 265.
items.proposal: The aim of the system must be clear to everyone in the system. [*What is the system for? What should it be attempting to do? For, without clarity on such matters, on what could decisions be sensibly based?*] Without an aim, there is no system. [*There couldn't be a system if neither management nor their staff really understand what they are supposed to be trying to do, nor why! On what could they "work together"?*] The aim is a value-judgment. [*I.e. the aim or purpose of the system is subjective. As Deming said at the 1990 presentation to senior executives:* ["The aim of a system is not a theorem: you don't derive it from axioms and corollaries."]{.deming_quote} *See* Deming Speaks to European Executives*, BDA Booklet A10 page 8 and* DemDim *page 265.*]
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p5 — and the image also shows the direct Deming quote (“The aim of a system is not a theorem...”) rendered in the same blue used for Deming's own words elsewhere on the page, distinct from the surrounding black italic of Neave's bracket. Two defects compound here: (1) “nor why!” is dropped from the previous sentence, and (2) the whole clause “the aim or purpose of the system is subjective. As Deming said at the 1990 presentation to senior executives:” is dropped, which also strips the quotation marks and attribution from the Deming quote that follows — the site currently presents “i.e. the aim of the system is not a theorem...” as Neave's own paraphrase rather than a quoted Deming line. The proposal restores both drops and marks the quoted sentence with {.deming_quote}, matching the convention already used elsewhere in this same file (line 81's ["The aim proposed here ... is for everybody to gain."]{.deming_quote}).

items.site_html: If the aim, size, or boundary of the organisation changes, then the functions of the components will for optimisation of the new system <mark class='gone'>need to</mark> change.
items.proposal: If the aim, size, or boundary of the organisation changes, then the functions of the components will for optimisation of the new system [*need to*] change. The site currently drops both the brackets and the italics, so “need to” silently reads as part of Deming's own May 1990 wording rather than Neave's editorial completion of it.

items.chip: “other well-designed systems” narrowed; “to” added that isn't in the source
items.source_html: [Clearly so if the components are human, but also more broadly in <mark class='src'>other well-designed systems</mark>.] ... Their aim <mark class='src'>is challenge</mark> for self-satisfaction, and to provide pleasure to listeners.
items.site_html: [Clearly so if the components are human, but also more broadly in <mark class='gone'>any well-designed system</mark>.] ... Their aim <mark class='gone'>is to challenge</mark> for self-satisfaction, and to provide pleasure to listeners.
items.proposal: The components of a system could in principle, under stable conditions, manage themselves to accomplish their aim. [*Clearly so if the components are human, but also more broadly in other well-designed systems.*] A possible example is a string quartet. Each of the four members supports the other three. None of them is there to attract individual attention. Four simultaneous solos do not make a string quartet. They practise singly and together, to accomplish their aim. Their aim is challenge for self-satisfaction, and to provide pleasure to listeners.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p8, character for character: the source really does read “other well-designed systems” (plural) and “Their aim is challenge for self-satisfaction” with no “to” — an odd but genuine construction in Neave's own text, not a pdftotext dropped word. The site's “any well-designed system” (singular) narrows the claim, and its added “to” silently smooths over a wording quirk that exact transcription calls for keeping.

The site instead links this to Day 9 page 2 — wrong day and wrong page, and coincidentally the same wrong anchor as D10-04's error, in the opposite direction: D10-04 needed a cross-day link and got a same-page one dropped; this one needed a same-day link and got sent to Day 9.

items.chip: Neave's “wibble-wobble” callback broken; several word/punctuation changes
items.source_html: ...no reason for the <mark class='src'>changes: I</mark> felt the same, was doing the same <mark class='src'>kind</mark> of things ... no trends or any kind of patterns apparent in <mark class='src'>the data: the</mark> numbers simply varied up and down ... invariably that has brought the variation back to <mark class='src'>“wibble-wobble” again</mark>. ... These are what Deming calls “common” causes <mark class='src'>of variation: I've</mark> learned that every system has them.
items.site_html: ...no reason for the <mark class='gone'>change. I</mark> felt the same, was doing the same <mark class='gone'>kinds</mark> of things ... no trends or any kind of patterns apparent in <mark class='gone'>the data. The</mark> numbers simply varied up and down ... invariably that has brought the variation back to <mark class='gone'>“stable system” behaviour</mark>. ... These are what Deming calls “common” causes <mark class='gone'>of variation. I've</mark> learned that every system has them.
items.proposal:
First, I found that my blood pressure varied quite a lot from day to day even when there seemed to be no reason for the changes: I felt the same, was doing the same kind of things, and took the readings at roughly the same time each day, etc. There were usually no trends or any kind of patterns apparent in the data: the numbers simply varied up and down, seemingly "at random", over a certain range. A friend of mine refers to that kind of variation as "wibble-wobble"! I can't remember what that range was so long ago: nowadays my systolic blood pressure is almost always between 120 and 150.

Just now and again I get a value outside that range, usually on the high side. When that happens I can often understand a good reason for it, e.g. I'm particularly excited or stressed about something, or I'm suffering from some kind of bug. But occasionally, over the 35 and more years, I've started getting some high values that I can't explain, or even see a slow trend upwards. When that happens I've shown my doctor the graphs and she has changed my medication, and invariably that has brought the variation back to "wibble-wobble" again.

The "wibble-wobble" situation is what Deming refers to in this item as a "stable system". There are bound to be *some* reasons for the ups and downs (else presumably the blood pressure would stay the same, day after day), but they are probably so many and various---and small---that nobody could identify their individual effects. These are what Deming calls "common" causes of variation: I've learned that every system has them. Causes of variation outside the usual range, or causes which actually change the behaviour of the variation from what it has been over recent readings, are what he calls "special" causes.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p20, across all three paragraphs of Neave's personal blood-pressure story. The one substantive change is the most damaging: Neave sets up “wibble-wobble” as a callback term two paragraphs earlier and pays it off with “brought the variation back to 'wibble-wobble' again” — the site instead substitutes “brought the variation back to 'stable system' behaviour”, breaking the callback the whole anecdote is building toward (the payoff sentence right after is “The 'wibble-wobble' situation is what Deming refers to ... as a 'stable system'”, which only makes sense as a payoff if “wibble-wobble” was just used again). The rest are smaller: “kind”→“kinds”, and three places where the source's colon joining two clauses into one sentence becomes a period splitting it into two (“changes: I felt”→“change. I felt”, “data: the numbers”→“data. The numbers”, “variation: I've learned”→“variation. I've learned”).

items.chip: “When do data” reversed to “When no data”
items.source_html: Understanding of the capability of a process. <mark class='src'>When do data indicate</mark> that a process is stable?
items.site_html: Understanding of the capability of a process. <mark class='gone'>When no data indicate</mark> that a process is stable?
items.proposal: 3. Understanding of the capability of a process. When do data indicate that a process is stable? The distribution of the output of a stable system is predictable with a high degree of belief. A process that is stable, in the state of statistical control, has a definable capability.
items.evidence_html: Confirmed on the page image, printed p22, in blue as Deming's own numbered item 3. “When do data indicate that a process is stable?” is a real, answerable question (item 3's whole point, expanded in the next two sentences); “When no data indicate that a process is stable?” does not parse as a sensible question at all — a one-word flip that turns Deming's point into nonsense.
